questions.prompt: What is disaster recovery?
options: Restoring IT systems after a disruption
Choosing a safe site for a new building
Classifying assets by how sensitive they are
Keeping the whole organization running

questions.prompt: What does RTO measure?
options: The maximum time a system can be down
The maximum data you can afford to lose
The time between two backup jobs
The number of backups kept off site

questions.prompt: What does RPO measure?
options: The cost of one hour of downtime
The number of copies kept on different media
The most data you can lose, in time
The longest time a system may stay offline

questions.prompt: The last backup was 45 minutes old when the failure hit. Up to how much data is lost?
options: None at all
4.5 hours
45 minutes
45 seconds

questions.prompt: The RTO is 2 hours and the relay was down for 3 hours. Was the target met?
options: Only partly
It depends on RPO
No
Yes

questions.prompt: The RPO is 1 hour and the last backup was 30 minutes old. Was the target met?
options: It depends on RTO
No
Only partly
Yes

questions.prompt: Where should RTO and RPO targets come from?
options: The smallest number that sounds good
Whatever another crew happens to use
A real look at cost and impact
A guess made during the outage itself

questions.prompt: Why not set every RTO and RPO as small as possible?
options: Small targets are against the law
Tighter targets cost more to reach
Backups stop working below one hour
Small targets make systems slower

questions.prompt: How is business continuity planning different from disaster recovery?
options: BCP only covers the backups kept off site
BCP keeps the whole organization running
BCP and DR mean exactly the same thing
BCP restores IT systems after a disruption happens

questions.prompt: Which activity belongs to business continuity, not disaster recovery?
options: Replacing a failed hard drive in a server
Restoring a database from last night's backup copy
Bringing a crashed server back online
An alternate place to work if the site is gone

questions.prompt: Backup personnel who can step into a critical role belong to which plan?
options: Asset classification
Business continuity
Disaster recovery
Change management

questions.prompt: Which question does BCP ask?
options: How do we keep operating at all?
How do we stop every attack?
How do we classify each file?
How do we get the systems back up?

questions.prompt: What does the 3 in the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
options: Three backups taken per day
Three copies of the data
Three sites for servers
Three people check it

questions.prompt: What does the 2 in the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
options: Two backups are taken every single hour
Two different types of storage media
Two copies are kept on the same drive
Two people must approve each backup

questions.prompt: What does the 1 in the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
options: One admin password
One copy kept offsite
One backup per year
One drive for all data

questions.prompt: Why keep one copy offsite?
options: Offsite copies are faster to restore
Offsite copies never need testing
The law forbids keeping copies onsite
One disaster can't destroy every copy

questions.prompt: Why can't an untested backup be trusted?
options: Failures hide until you restore
Testing makes the backup much smaller
Untested backups are against the rule
Untested backups are always deleted

questions.prompt: A backup job has been silently failing for weeks. How is this usually found?
options: By restoring and checking a backup
By reading the backup's file name aloud
By waiting for the next disaster
By buying a second backup drive

questions.prompt: What is high availability?
options: Restoring data from a backup after a failure
Keeping a system running when one part fails
Keeping one copy of the data off site
Checking a plan against a regulation

questions.prompt: What is a single point of failure?
options: A part that has a working backup beside it
A backup that is stored in only one place
A failure that happens only one time ever
One part whose failure stops everything

questions.prompt: What removes a single point of failure?
options: A single backup
A longer password
A stricter policy
Redundancy

questions.prompt: Why add load balancing to redundant parts?
options: RPO gets a lot longer
Backups get much smaller
Logs get shorter each day
Failover becomes instant

questions.prompt: How do backups and high availability differ?
options: HA prevents downtime; backups recover data after it
Backups prevent downtime; HA recovers data after it
They are the same thing with two different names
HA only works if there are no backups at all

questions.prompt: The whole Citadel loses contact when one relay fails. What is that relay?
options: A single point of failure
An offsite backup copy
A load balancer pair
A compliance record entry

questions.prompt: What does auditing a DR plan mean?
options: Checking the plan and evidence against requirements
Deleting old plans so only the newest one remains
Trusting the plan is fine because it is written down
Rewriting the plan from scratch every single month

questions.prompt: A DR plan is detailed and well written but has never been tested. Is it compliant?
options: Yes
Mostly
Only on paper
No

questions.prompt: What do most standards require for a DR plan?
options: A plan that is at least fifty pages long in total
A signature from every single crew member
Documented proof of a real test in a set period
A copy of the plan printed and kept on the wall

questions.prompt: "We have a plan" and "we tested this plan and it worked" — how do they differ?
options: They are the same claim
Only the first counts in an audit
Only the second is real evidence
Neither one matters to auditors

questions.prompt: What should be kept after a DR test?
options: Only the backup file that was used
A written record of the test and result
Only the name of the person who ran it
Nothing, since the test is enough by itself

questions.prompt: A tighter RPO usually needs what?
options: Less storage space
Fewer backup copies
More frequent backups
A longer outage window
